chunks.text: business objective: The system allows customers to apply for loans online, upload the required documents, verify their information, track application status, and receive an approval or rejection decision without visiting a bank. users and roles: Customers can submit loan applications, upload documents, and track their application status. Loan officers can review applications, verify documents, and approve or reject loans. Administrators can manage users, configure loan policies, and monitor the system. workflow and outcomes: The application starts when a customer submits a loan application with personal details, employment information, requested loan amount, income, and required documents.

The system validates the submitted information and checks whether all mandatory documents are provided. It then performs eligibility checks based on income, credit score, loan amount, and existing obligations. If the applicant satisfies the eligibility criteria, the application is approved or sent to a loan officer for final review. If the applicant does not satisfy the criteria, the application is rejected with the reason for rejection. The applicant should receive the application status and decision through the online portal. exceptions: If required information is missing, the system should identify the missing fields and ask the customer to provide them before processing the application.

If submitted documents are invalid or cannot be verified, the application should be sent to a loan officer for manual review. If the applicant fails the eligibility checks, the application should be rejected and the applicant should receive the reason for rejection. Technical failures should not result in an incorrect approval or rejection; the application should be placed in a pending state and retried or reviewed manually. Loan officers own manual reviews and can override automated decisions when justified, with the reason for the override recorded. Administrators handle system-level failures and configuration issues.

business rules: If required information is missing, the system should identify the missing fields and ask the customer to provide them before processing the application. If submitted documents are invalid or cannot be verified, the application should be sent to a loan officer for manual review. If the applicant fails the eligibility checks, the application should be rejected and the applicant should receive the reason for rejection. Technical failures should not result in an incorrect approval or rejection; the application should be placed in a pending state and retried or reviewed manually.

Loan officers own manual reviews and can override automated decisions when justified, with the reason for the override recorded. Administrators handle system-level failures and configuration issues. data and integrations: The system collects customer personal details, employment and income information, loan details, identity documents, credit information, and application status. It exchanges data with the bank's customer database, credit bureau, document verification service, and notification service. The credit bureau is used to obtain credit scores and existing loan information, while the document verification service validates submitted identity and income documents.

If an external integration is unavailable, the application should not be automatically approved or rejected. It should remain pending, retry the integration when possible, and be sent for manual review if the issue persists. All important integration failures should be logged. security and compliance: Access should be based on role-based permissions. Customers should only access their own applications and documents. Loan officers should access applications assigned to them, while administrators should have controlled access to system configuration and audit information.

All important actions such as application submission, document access, approval, rejection, and manual overrides should be recorded in an audit log with the user, timestamp, and action. Personal and financial information must be encrypted during transmission and storage. The system should protect sensitive customer data, perform fraud and identity verification checks, enforce secure authentication, and comply with applicable financial and data privacy regulations. Access to sensitive information should be logged and restricted to authorized users.

service levels and scale: The system should support around 10,000 loan applications per day, with peak traffic of approximately 1,000 applications per hour during business hours. Normal application pages and API requests should respond within 2–3 seconds, while document verification and credit checks may take longer because they depend on external services. The system should target 99.9% availability. If a service fails, applications should remain safely stored and recover without data loss. Failed integrations should be retried, and unresolved applications should be placed in a pending state for manual review.
The system should support scaling as the number of customers and applications increases. delivery constraints: no idea validation and rollout: no idea

factors.name: Requirement stability
factors.rationale: Draft or unapproved requirements indicate that stability has not yet been demonstrated.

factors.name: Requirement clarity
factors.rationale: Measured from the presence of concrete, non-placeholder acceptance criteria.

factors.name: Risk
factors.rationale: Derived from stated high risk and security, privacy, regulatory, or audit classifications.

factors.name: Complexity
factors.rationale: Integration and data-management requirements increase coordination and technical complexity.

factors.name: Need for early prototype
factors.rationale: Unclear requirements or integration complexity make early learning and validation valuable.

factors.name: Time constraints
factors.rationale: No schedule or deadline evidence is available in the generated requirements; confirm this with the project sponsor.

factors.name: Customer involvement
factors.rationale: Derived only from business, stakeholder, or usability requirements; otherwise this must be confirmed.

factors.name: Frequency of changes
factors.rationale: Requirement documents do not establish the expected change rate; confirm with product and business stakeholders.

factors.name: Need for iterative development
factors.rationale: Unapproved or unclear requirements benefit from repeated review and validation cycles.

factors.name: Need for risk analysis
factors.rationale: Security/compliance concerns or complex integration warrant explicit risk analysis.

options.name: Spiral
options.suitability: Best when risk analysis, prototypes, and repeated risk-reduction cycles are central.

options.name: Prototyping
options.suitability: Best for validating uncertain user needs, workflows, and interfaces before committing to a full build.

options.name: Agile
options.suitability: Best for frequent feedback and evolving requirements, with planned governance for high-risk work.

options.name: Incremental
options.suitability: Best when value can be divided into validated, independently testable increments.

options.name: V-Shape
options.suitability: Best when each specification stage needs a linked verification and validation activity.

options.name: RAD
options.suitability: Best for time-boxed delivery with available users and modular, lower-risk scope.

options.name: Waterfall
options.suitability: Best when requirements are stable, fully specified, and changes are controlled.

sdlc.justification: Spiral has the highest transparent score because requirement stability is needs validation, requirement clarity is low, risk is high, complexity is high, need for early prototype is likely.
